properly report failure to deliver if delivery cannot be completed

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Contemporary SMTP implementations MUST support the basic extension mechanisms.

actions: accept and process EHLO command regardless of extension support

statements.description: (However, for compatibility with older conforming implementations, SMTP clients and servers MUST support the original HELO mechanisms as a fallback.)
actions: support HELO as a fallback session-initiation mechanism

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Each service extension registered with the IANA must be defined in a formal Standards-Track or IESG-approved Experimental protocol document.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: The definition must include: o  the textual name of the SMTP service extension; o  the EHLO keyword value associated with the extension; o  the syntax and possible values of parameters associated with the EHLO keyword value; o  any additional SMTP verbs associated with the extension (additional verbs will usually be, but are not required to be, the same as the EHLO keyword value); o  any new parameters the extension associates with the MAIL or RCPT verbs; o  a description of how support for the extension affects the behavior of a server and client SMTP; and o  the increment by which the extension is increasing the maximum length of the commands MAIL and/or RCPT, over that specified in this Standard.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Keywords beginning with "X" MUST NOT be used in a registered service extension.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Conversely, keyword values presented in the EHLO response that do not begin with "X" MUST correspond to a Standard, Standards-Track, or IESG-approved Experimental SMTP service extension registered with IANA.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: A conforming server MUST NOT offer non-"X"-prefixed keyword values that are not described in a registered extension.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Additional verbs and parameter names are bound by the same rules as EHLO keywords; specifically, verbs beginning with "X" are local extensions that may not be registered or standardized.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Conversely, verbs not beginning with "X" must always be registered.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In particular, if an extension implies that the delivery path normally supports special features of that extension, and an intermediate SMTP system finds a next hop that does not support the required extension, it MAY choose, based on the specific extension and circumstances, to requeue the message and try later and/or try an alternate MX host.

statements.subject: timer
statements.description: If this strategy is employed, the timeout to fall back to an unextended format (if one is available) SHOULD be less than the normal timeout for bouncing as undeliverable (e.g., if normal timeout is three days, the requeue timeout before attempting to transmit the mail without the extension might be one day).
actions: configure fallback-to-unextended timeout to be less than bounce-as-undeliverable timeout
attempt transmission without extension upon timeout expiry

statements.subject: message
statements.description: It consists of an originator address (to which error reports should be directed), one or more recipient addresses, and optional protocol extension material.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Although SMTP extensions (such as "8BITMIME", RFC 1652 [22]) may relax this restriction for the content body, the content header fields are always encoded using the US-ASCII repertoire.

statements.subject: endpoint
statements.description: Hosts are known by names (see the next section); they SHOULD NOT be identified by numerical addresses, i.e., by address literals as described in Section 4.1.2.

statements.subject: transaction
statements.description: Local aliases MUST NOT appear in any SMTP transaction.

statements.subject: participant
statements.description: Local nicknames or unqualified names MUST NOT be used.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: The domain name given in the EHLO command MUST be either a primary host name (a domain name that resolves to an address RR) or, if the host has no name, an address literal, as described in Section 4.1.3 and discussed further in the EHLO discussion of Section 4.1.4.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: The reserved mailbox name "postmaster" may be used in a RCPT command without domain qualification (see Section 4.1.1.3) and MUST be accepted if so used.

statements.subject: participant
statements.description: Conforming implementations MUST NOT recognize or generate any other character or character sequence as a line terminator.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Limits MAY be imposed on line lengths by servers (see Section 4).

statements.subject: client
statements.description: SMTP client implementations MUST NOT transmit these characters except when they are intended as line terminators and then MUST, as indicated above, transmit them only as a <CRLF> sequence.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: For the purposes of this specification, firewalls that rewrite addresses should be considered as gateways, even if SMTP is used on both sides of them (see RFC 2979 [27]).

statements.subject: server
statements.description: the local-part MUST be interpreted and assigned semantics only by the host specified in the domain part of the address.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: That is, a command verb, an argument value other than a mailbox local-part, and free form text MAY be encoded in upper case, lower case, or any mixture of upper and lower case with no impact on its meaning.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: The local-part of a mailbox MUST BE treated as case sensitive.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Therefore, SMTP implementations MUST take care to preserve the case of mailbox local-parts.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Implementations MAY wish to employ this encoding to accommodate those servers.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: An originating SMTP client that has not successfully negotiated an appropriate extension with a particular server (see the next paragraph) MUST NOT transmit messages with information in the high-order bit of octets.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If such messages are transmitted in violation of this rule, receiving SMTP servers MAY clear the high-order bit or reject the message as invalid.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In general, a relay SMTP SHOULD assume that the message content it has received is valid and, assuming that the envelope permits doing so, relay it without inspecting that content.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Delivery SMTP systems MAY reject such messages, or return them as undeliverable, rather than deliver them.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Receiving systems SHOULD reject such commands, normally using "500 syntax error - invalid character" replies.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: 8-bit message content transmission MAY be requested of the server by a client using extended SMTP facilities, notably the "8BITMIME" extension, RFC 1652 [22].

statements.subject: server
statements.description: 8BITMIME SHOULD be supported by SMTP servers.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: However, it MUST NOT be construed as authorization to transmit unrestricted 8-bit material, nor does 8BITMIME authorize transmission of any envelope material in other than ASCII.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: 8BITMIME MUST NOT be requested by senders for material with the high bit on that is not in MIME format with an appropriate content-transfer encoding; servers MAY reject such messages.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: SMTP server implementations MAY include identification of their software and version information in the connection greeting reply after the 220 code, a practice that permits more efficient isolation and repair of any problems.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Implementations MAY make provision for SMTP servers to disable the software and version announcement where it causes security concerns.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: a 554 response MAY be given in the initial connection opening message instead of the 220.
actions: send 554 response in connection opening message instead of 220

statements.subject: server
statements.description: A server taking this approach MUST still wait for the client to send a QUIT (see Section 4.1.1.10) before closing the connection and SHOULD respond to any intervening commands with "503 bad sequence of commands".
actions: wait for client to send QUIT before closing connection

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Since an attempt to make an SMTP connection to such a system is probably in error, a server returning a 554 response on connection opening SHOULD provide enough information in the reply text to facilitate debugging of the sending system.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Older SMTP systems that are unable to support service extensions, and contemporary clients that do not require service extensions in the mail session being initiated, MAY use HELO instead of EHLO.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Servers MUST NOT return the extended EHLO-style response to a HELO command.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: For a particular connection attempt, if the server returns a "command not recognized" response to EHLO, the client SHOULD be able to fall back and send HELO.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If the mailbox specification is not acceptable for some reason, the server MUST return a reply indicating whether the failure is permanent (i.e., will occur again if the client tries to send the same address again) or temporary (i.e., the address might be accepted if the client tries again later).
actions: return reply indicating whether failure is permanent or temporary

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In those cases, the server MAY reasonably accept the reverse-path (with a 250 reply) and then report problems after the forward-paths are received and examined.
actions: defer reverse-path problem reporting until RCPT examination

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Historically, the <reverse-path> was permitted to contain more than just a mailbox; however, contemporary systems SHOULD NOT use source routing (see Appendix C).

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Historically, the <forward-path> was permitted to contain a source routing list of hosts and the destination mailbox; however, contemporary SMTP clients SHOULD NOT utilize source routes (see Appendix C).

actions: accept and process RCPT command containing source routes in forward-path without rejecting solely for their presence

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Similarly, servers MAY decline to accept mail that is destined for other hosts or systems.
actions: decline to accept RCPT for mail destined to other hosts or systems

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Consequently, restricted-capability clients MUST NOT assume that any SMTP server on the Internet can be used as their mail processing (relaying) site.

actions: send 503 Bad sequence of commands response

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If there was no MAIL, or no RCPT, command, or all such commands were rejected, the server MAY return a "command out of sequence" (503) or "no valid recipients" (554) reply in response to the DATA command.
actions: send 503 command out of sequence reply or 554 no valid recipients reply

statements.subject: client
statements.description: If one of those replies (or any other 5yz reply) is received, the client MUST NOT send the message data; more generally, message data MUST NOT be sent unless a 354 reply is received.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: These servers SHOULD treat a failure for one or more recipients as a "subsequent failure" and return a mail message as discussed in Section 6 and, in particular, in Section 6.1.
actions: classify recipient delivery failure as subsequent failure
return bounce mail message per Section 6

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Server SMTP systems SHOULD NOT reject messages based on perceived defects in the RFC 822 or MIME (RFC 2045 [21]) message header section or message body.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In particular, they MUST NOT reject messages in which the numbers of Resent-header fields do not match or Resent-to appears without Resent-from and/or Resent-date.

statements.subject: transaction
statements.description: Mail transaction commands MUST be used in the order discussed above.
actions: issue MAIL before any RCPT command

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Servers MAY forward messages when they are aware of an address change.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: When they do so, they MAY either provide address-updating information with a 251 code, or may forward "silently" and return a 250 code.
actions: OR forward silently and send 250 reply

statements.subject: server
statements.description: However, if a 251 code is used, they MUST NOT assume that the client will actually update address information or even return that information to the user.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Servers MAY reject messages or return them as non-deliverable when they cannot be delivered precisely as addressed.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: When they do so, they MAY either provide address-updating information with a 551 code, or may reject the message as undeliverable with a 550 code and no address-specific information.
actions: OR send 550 reply with no address-specific information

statements.subject: server
statements.description: However, if a 551 code is used, they MUST NOT assume that the client will actually update address information or even return that information to the user.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: SMTP server implementations that support the 251 and/or 551 reply codes SHOULD provide configuration mechanisms so that sites that conclude that they would undesirably disclose information can disable or restrict their use.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Implementations SHOULD support VRFY and EXPN (however, see Section 3.5.2 and Section 7.3).

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If a normal (i.e., 250) response is returned, the response MAY include the full name of the user and MUST include the mailbox of the user.
actions: optionally include full name of user in 250 response

statements.subject: server
statements.description: It MUST be in either of the following forms:

statements.subject: server
statements.description: When a name that is the argument to VRFY could identify more than one mailbox, the server MAY either note the ambiguity or identify the alternatives.
actions: or return 553 response listing alternative mailboxes

statements.subject: server
statements.description: For the EXPN command, the string identifies a mailing list, and the successful (i.e., 250) multiline response MAY include the full name of the users and MUST give the mailboxes on the mailing list.
actions: optionally include full name of users in 250 multiline response

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If a request is made to apply VRFY to a mailing list, a positive response MAY be given if a message so addressed would be delivered to everyone on the list, otherwise an error SHOULD be reported (e.g., "550 That is a mailing list, not a user" or "252 Unable to verify members of mailing list").
actions: return positive response to VRFY for mailing list

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If a request is made to expand a user name, the server MAY return a positive response consisting of a list containing one name, or an error MAY be reported (e.g., "550 That is a user name, not a mailing list").
actions: return positive response with single-name list

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: An implementation of the VRFY or EXPN commands MUST include at least recognition of local mailboxes as "user names".

statements.subject: server
statements.description: However, since current Internet practice often results in a single host handling mail for multiple domains, hosts, especially hosts that provide this functionality, SHOULD accept the "local-part@domain" form as a "user name"; hosts MAY also choose to recognize other strings as "user names".

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Similarly, historical variations in what is returned by these commands are such that the response SHOULD be interpreted very carefully, if at all, and SHOULD generally only be used for diagnostic purposes.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: When normal (2yz or 551) responses are returned from a VRFY or EXPN request, the reply MUST include the <Mailbox> name using a "<local-part@domain>" construction, where "domain" is a fully-qualified domain name.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In circumstances exceptional enough to justify violating the intent of this specification, free-form text MAY be returned.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: In order to facilitate parsing by both computers and people, addresses SHOULD appear in pointed brackets.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: When addresses, rather than free-form debugging information, are returned, EXPN and VRFY MUST return only valid domain addresses that are usable in SMTP RCPT commands.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Consequently, if an address implies delivery to a program or other system, the mailbox name used to reach that target MUST be given.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Paths (explicit source routes) MUST NOT be returned by VRFY or EXPN.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Server implementations SHOULD support both VRFY and EXPN.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: For security reasons, implementations MAY provide local installations a way to disable either or both of these commands through configuration options or the equivalent (see Section 7.3).

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Since they were both optional in RFC 821, but VRFY was made mandatory in RFC 1123 [3], if EXPN is supported, it MUST be listed as a service extension in an EHLO response.
actions: include EXPN in EHLO extensions list in response

statements.subject: server
statements.description: VRFY MAY be listed as a convenience but, since support for it is required, SMTP clients are not required to check for its presence on the extension list before using it.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: A server MUST NOT return a 250 code in response to a VRFY or EXPN command unless it has actually verified the address.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In particular, a server MUST NOT return 250 if all it has done is to verify that the syntax given is valid.
actions: prohibit sending 250 response code when only syntax was verified

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In that case, 502 (Command not implemented) or 500 (Syntax error, command unrecognized) SHOULD be returned.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In these situations, reply code 252 SHOULD be returned.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Implementations generally SHOULD be more aggressive about address verification in the case of VRFY than in the case of RCPT, even if it takes a little longer to do so.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: mail systems SHOULD NOT attempt them.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: SMTP clients SHOULD NOT generate explicit source routes except under unusual circumstances.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: SMTP servers MAY decline to act as mail relays or to accept addresses that specify source routes.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: When route information is encountered, SMTP servers MAY ignore the route information and simply send to the final destination specified as the last element in the route and SHOULD do so.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: This is one of several reasons why SMTP clients MUST NOT generate invalid source routes or depend on serial resolution of names.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If it declines to relay mail to a particular address for policy reasons, a 550 response SHOULD be returned.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: A server MAY attempt to verify the return path before using its address for delivery notifications, but methods of doing so are not defined here nor is any particular method recommended at this time.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If an SMTP server has accepted the task of relaying the mail and later finds that the destination is incorrect or that the mail cannot be delivered for some other reason, then it MUST construct an "undeliverable mail" notification message and send it to the originator of the undeliverable mail (as indicated by the reverse-path).
actions: Send notification message to originator as indicated by reverse-path

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Formats specified for non-delivery reports by other standards (see, for example, RFC 3461 [32] and RFC 3464 [33]) SHOULD be used if possible.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Of course, SMTP servers MUST NOT send notification messages about problems transporting notification messages.
actions: Do not send notification message in response to notification transport failure

statements.subject: server
statements.description: When such a message is transmitted, the reverse-path MUST be set to null (see Section 4.5.5 for additional discussion).
actions: Set reverse-path to null in MAIL command of notification message

statements.subject: server
statements.description: As discussed in Section 6.4, a relay SMTP has no need to inspect or act upon the header section or body of the message data and MUST NOT do so except to add its own "Received:" header field (Section 4.4) and, optionally, to attempt to detect looping in the mail system (see Section 6.3).
statements.post_cond: header_section.inspected = false & body.inspected = false & header_section.modified = false & body.modified = false
actions: Do not inspect or act upon header section or body of message data
Optionally attempt to detect looping in the mail system

statements.subject: message
statements.description: Header fields MAY be rewritten when necessary as messages are gatewayed across mail environment boundaries.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: When forwarding a message into or out of the Internet environment, a gateway MUST prepend a Received: line, but it MUST NOT alter in any way a Received: line that is already in the header section.
statements.trigger: forwarding message into or out of Internet environment
actions: prepend Received: line to message header section

statements.subject: server
statements.description: receiving systems MUST NOT reject mail based on the format of a trace header field and SHOULD be extremely robust in the light of unexpected information or formats in those header fields.
statements.trigger: receipt of mail with non-conforming trace header field format
actions: do not issue rejection response solely on grounds of trace header field format non-conformance

statements.subject: server
statements.description: The gateway SHOULD indicate the environment and protocol in the "via" clauses of Received header field(s) that it supplies.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: From the Internet side, the gateway SHOULD accept all valid address formats in SMTP commands and in the RFC 822 header section, and all valid RFC 822 messages.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: Addresses and header fields generated by gateways MUST conform to applicable standards (including this one and RFC 5322 [4]).

statements.subject: message
statements.description: The gateway MUST ensure that all header fields of a message that it forwards into the Internet mail environment meet the requirements for Internet mail.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: In particular, all addresses in "From:", "To:", "Cc:", etc., header fields MUST be transformed (if necessary) to satisfy the standard header syntax of RFC 5322 [4], MUST reference only fully-qualified domain names, and MUST be effective and useful for sending replies.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: The translation algorithm used to convert mail from the Internet protocols to another environment's protocol SHOULD ensure that error messages from the foreign mail environment are delivered to the reverse-path from the SMTP envelope, not to an address in the "From:", "Sender:", or similar header fields of the message.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: when forwarding a message from another environment into the Internet, the gateway SHOULD set the envelope return path in accordance with an error message return address, if supplied by the foreign environment.
actions: set envelope return path to foreign environment error message return address

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If the foreign environment has no equivalent concept, the gateway must select and use a best approximation, with the message originator's address as the default of last resort.
actions: select best approximation for envelope return path
use message originator address as return path default of last resort

statements.subject: server
statements.description: An SMTP server MUST NOT intentionally close the connection under normal operational circumstances (see Section 7.8) except: o  After receiving a QUIT command and responding with a 221 reply. o  After detecting the need to shut down the SMTP service and returning a 421 response code.  This response code can be issued after the server receives any command or, if necessary, asynchronously from command receipt (on the assumption that the client will receive it after the next command is issued). o  After a timeout, as specified in Section 4.5.3.2, occurs waiting for the client to send a command or data.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: An SMTP server that is forcibly shut down via external means SHOULD attempt to send a line containing a 421 response code to the SMTP client before exiting.
actions: send a line containing a 421 response code to the SMTP client before exiting

statements.description: SMTP clients that experience a connection close, reset, or other communications failure due to circumstances not under their control (in violation of the intent of this specification but sometimes unavoidable) SHOULD, to maintain the robustness of the mail system, treat the mail transaction as if a 451 response had been received and act accordingly.
actions: treat the mail transaction as if a 451 response had been received

statements.subject: server
statements.description: An SMTP-capable host SHOULD support both the alias and the list models of address expansion for multiple delivery.

actions: Set envelope MAIL FROM to list administrator address before forwarding each copy

statements.subject: message
statements.description: However, in this case, the message header section (RFC 5322 [4]) MUST be left unchanged; in particular, the "From" field of the header section is unaffected.
actions: Leave message header section unchanged when forwarding to expanded list

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Servers SHOULD simply utilize the addresses on the list; application of heuristics or other matching rules to eliminate some addresses, such as that of the originator, is strongly discouraged.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: (In the interest of improved interoperability, SMTP receivers SHOULD tolerate trailing white space before the terminating <CRLF>.)
actions: tolerate trailing white space before terminating <CRLF>

statements.subject: message
statements.description: The syntax of the local part of a mailbox MUST conform to receiver site conventions and the syntax specified in Section 4.1.2.

statements.description: In the absence of specific extensions offered by the server and accepted by the client, clients MUST NOT send such parameters and servers SHOULD reject commands containing them as having invalid syntax.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: In situations in which the SMTP client system does not have a meaningful domain name (e.g., when its address is dynamically allocated and no reverse mapping record is available), the client SHOULD send an address literal (see Section 4.1.3).

statements.subject: client
statements.description: In the interest of interoperability, it is probably wise for servers to be prepared for this string to occur, but SMTP clients SHOULD NOT send it.

statements.description: Older client SMTP systems MAY, as discussed above, use HELO (as specified in RFC 821) instead of EHLO, and servers MUST support the HELO command and reply properly to it.
actions: send HELO command instead of EHLO

statements.subject: client
statements.description: In any event, a client MUST issue HELO or EHLO before starting a mail transaction.
actions: issue HELO or EHLO command before initiating mail transaction

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Although EHLO keywords may be specified in upper, lower, or mixed case, they MUST always be recognized and processed in a case-insensitive manner.

statements.description: The EHLO response MUST contain keywords (and associated parameters if required) for all commands not listed as "required" in Section 4.5.1 excepting only private-use commands as described in Section 4.1.5.
actions: include all supported non-required extension keywords in EHLO response

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Private-use commands MAY be listed.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: The argument clause contains a reverse-path and may contain optional parameters.

statements.description: If service extensions were negotiated, the MAIL command may also carry parameters associated with a particular service extension.

statements.description: As provided in Appendix C, xyz.com MAY also choose to relay the message to hosta.int, using the envelope commands MAIL FROM:<userx@y.foo.org> RCPT TO:<@hosta.int,@jkl.org:userc@d.bar.org> or to jkl.org, using the envelope commands MAIL FROM:<userx@y.foo.org> RCPT TO:<@jkl.org:userc@d.bar.org>

statements.subject: client
statements.description: The client MUST NOT transmit parameters other than those associated with a service extension offered by the server in its EHLO response.

statements.description: The mail data may contain any of the 128 ASCII character codes, although experience has indicated that use of control characters other than SP, HT, CR, and LF may cause problems and SHOULD be avoided when possible.

statements.subject: server

statements.description: If it determines that it should relay the message without rewriting the address, it MUST sort the MX records to determine candidates for delivery.
actions: sort MX records by preference to determine delivery candidates

statements.subject: server
statements.description: The relay host MUST then inspect the list for any of the names or addresses by which it might be known in mail transactions.
actions: inspect sorted MX list for own names or addresses

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If a matching record is found, all records at that preference level and higher-numbered ones MUST be discarded from consideration.
actions: discard all MX records at matching preference level
discard all MX records at higher-numbered preference levels

statements.subject: message
statements.description: If there are no records left at that point, it is an error condition, and the message MUST be returned as undeliverable.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If records do remain, they SHOULD be tried, best preference first, as described above.
actions: try remaining MX records in best-preference-first order

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: In the contemporary Internet, SMTP clients and servers may be hosted on IPv4 systems, IPv6 systems, or dual-stack systems that are compatible with either version of the Internet Protocol.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Designers of SMTP implementations that might run in IPv6 or dual-stack environments should study the procedures above, especially the comments about multihomed hosts, and, preferably, provide mechanisms to facilitate operational tuning and mail interoperability between IPv4 and IPv6 systems while considering local circumstances.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: It MUST NOT lose the message for frivolous reasons, such as because the host later crashes or because of a predictable resource shortage.
actions: do not discard message due to host crash
do not discard message due to predictable resource shortage

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If there is a delivery failure after acceptance of a message, the receiver-SMTP MUST formulate and mail a notification message.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: This notification MUST be sent using a null ("<>") reverse-path in the envelope.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: The recipient of this notification MUST be the address from the envelope return path (or the Return-Path: line).

statements.subject: server
statements.description: However, if this address is null ("<>"), the receiver-SMTP MUST NOT send a notification.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: If the address is an explicit source route, it MUST be stripped down to its final hop.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: The notification message MUST be sent using: RCPT TO:<user@d>

statements.subject: server
statements.description: To avoid receiving duplicate messages as the result of timeouts, a receiver-SMTP MUST seek to minimize the time required to respond to the final <CRLF>.<CRLF> end of data indicator.
actions: minimize processing time before responding to end-of-data indicator
send 250 OK promptly after receiving end-of-data sequence to prevent sender timeout and retransmission

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Utility and predictability of the Internet mail system requires that messages that can be delivered should be delivered, regardless of any syntax or other faults associated with those messages and regardless of their content.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If they cannot be delivered, and cannot be rejected by the SMTP server during the SMTP transaction, they should be "bounced" (returned with non-delivery notification messages) as described above.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: So silent dropping of messages should be considered only in those cases where there is very high confidence that the messages are seriously fraudulent or otherwise inappropriate.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: To stretch the principle of delivery if possible even further, it may be a rational policy to not deliver mail that has an invalid return address, although the history of the network is that users are typically better served by delivering any message that can be delivered.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Reliably determining that a return address is invalid can be a difficult and time-consuming process, especially if the putative sending system is not directly accessible or does not fully and accurately support VRFY and, even if a "drop messages with invalid return addresses" policy is adopted, it SHOULD be applied only when there is near-certainty that the return addresses are, in fact, invalid.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Conversely, if a message is rejected because it is found to contain hostile content (a decision that is outside the scope of an SMTP server as defined in this document), rejection ("bounce") messages SHOULD NOT be sent unless the receiving site is confident that those messages will be usefully delivered.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: SMTP servers using this technique SHOULD use a large rejection threshold, normally at least 100 Received entries.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Whatever mechanisms are used, servers MUST contain provisions for detecting and stopping trivial loops.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: The following changes to a message being processed MAY be applied when necessary by an originating SMTP server, or one used as the target of SMTP as an initial posting (message submission) protocol:
actions: add message-id field when none appears
add date, time, or time zone when none appears
correct addresses to proper FQDN format

statements.subject: server
statements.description: These changes MUST NOT be applied by an SMTP server that provides an intermediate relay function.
actions: prohibit addition of date, time, or time zone
prohibit correction of addresses to FQDN format

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In all cases, documentation SHOULD be provided in trace header fields and/or header field comments for actions performed by the servers.
actions: provide documentation of server actions in trace header fields and/or header field comments

statements.subject: server
statements.description: (Systems that provide convenient ways for users to alter these header fields on a per-message basis should attempt to establish a primary and permanent mailbox address for the user so that Sender header fields within the message data can be generated sensibly.)

statements.subject: participant
statements.description: Especially when more than one RCPT command is present, and in order to avoid defeating some of the purpose of these mechanisms, SMTP clients and servers SHOULD NOT copy the full set of RCPT command arguments into the header section, either as part of trace header fields or as informational or private-extension header fields.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: sending SMTP systems that are aware of "bcc" use MAY find it helpful to send each blind copy as a separate message transaction containing only a single RCPT command.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Receiving systems SHOULD NOT attempt to deduce such relationships and use them to alter the header section of the message for delivery.

statements.subject: participant
statements.description: The popular "Apparently-to" header field is a violation of this principle as well as a common source of unintended information disclosure and SHOULD NOT be used.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: As a corollary to the above, implementations that permit this MUST NOT appear to have verified addresses that are not, in fact, verified.
actions: Do not return a response code or reply text indicating that the address has been verified

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If a site disables these commands for security reasons, the SMTP server MUST return a 252 response, rather than a code that could be confused with successful or unsuccessful verification.
actions: Send 252 reply code in response to VRFY or EXPN command

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Implementations SHOULD still provide support for EXPN, but sites SHOULD carefully evaluate the tradeoffs.
actions: Process EXPN command and return appropriate response

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Before a client uses the 251 or 551 reply codes from a RCPT command to automatically update its future behavior (e.g., updating the user's address book), it should be certain of the server's authenticity.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: If it does not, it may be subject to a man in the middle attack.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: implementations SHOULD minimally provide for making type and version information available in some way to other network hosts.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: This ordinarily does not pose a problem, but sites with special concerns about name disclosure should be aware of it.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Also, the optional FOR clause should be supplied with caution or not at all when multiple recipients are involved lest it inadvertently disclose the identities of "blind copy" recipients to others.
actions: supply FOR clause with caution or omit FOR clause entirely from Received header

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Sites that are concerned about those issues should ensure that they select and configure servers appropriately.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: It is a well-established principle that an SMTP server may refuse to accept mail for any operational or technical reason that makes sense to the site providing the server.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: considerable care should be taken and balance maintained if a site decides to be selective about the traffic it will accept and process.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: implementations SHOULD provide the capability to perform this type of filtering.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: When mail is rejected for these or other policy reasons, a 550 code SHOULD be used in response to EHLO (or HELO), MAIL, or RCPT as appropriate.
actions: send 550 reply to the triggering command (EHLO, HELO, MAIL, or RCPT)

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: As specified in Section 2.2.2, no entry may be made in this registry that starts in an "X".

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Entries may be made only for service extensions (and associated keywords, parameters, or verbs) that are defined in Standards-Track or Experimental RFCs specifically approved by the IESG for this purpose.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: Link and protocol identifiers in addition to those specified in this document may be registered only by standardization or by way of an RFC-documented, IESG-approved, Experimental protocol extension.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: As new clauses are defined, they may, in principle, specify creation of their own registries if the Strings consist of reserved terms or keywords rather than less restricted strings.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: As with link and protocol identifiers, additional clauses may be registered only by standardization or by way of an RFC-documented, IESG-approved, Experimental protocol extension.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: In addition, if additional trace header fields (i.e., in addition to Return-path and Received) are ever created, those trace fields MUST be added to the IANA registry established by BCP 90 (RFC 3864) [11] for use with RFC 5322 [4].

statements.subject: client
statements.description: However, if the envelope is not supplied, SMTP commands SHOULD be generated as follows:
actions: generate SMTP commands from RFC 822 header fields

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Each recipient address from a TO, CC, or BCC header field SHOULD be copied to a RCPT command (generating multiple message copies if that is required for queuing or delivery).
actions: copy each recipient address from TO, CC, or BCC header fields to a RCPT command
generate multiple message copies if required for queuing or delivery

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Any BCC header fields SHOULD then be removed from the header section.
actions: remove all BCC header fields from the header section

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Once this process is completed, the remaining header fields SHOULD be checked to verify that at least one TO, CC, or BCC header field remains.
actions: check remaining header fields to verify at least one TO, CC, or BCC header field remains

statements.subject: client
statements.description: If none do, then a BCC header field with no additional information SHOULD be inserted as specified in [4].
statements.pre_cond: header.TO = absent & header.CC = absent & header.BCC = absent
actions: insert BCC header field with no additional information

statements.subject: client
statements.description: The return address in the MAIL command SHOULD, if possible, be derived from the system's identity for the submitting (local) user, and the "From:" header field otherwise.
actions: derive MAIL command return address from system identity if available, otherwise from From header field

statements.subject: client
statements.description: If there is a system identity available, it SHOULD also be copied to the Sender header field if it is different from the address in the From header field.
actions: copy system identity to Sender header field

statements.subject: client
statements.description: (Any Sender header field that was already there SHOULD be removed.)
actions: remove any pre-existing Sender header field

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: A submission protocol based on Standard RFC 822 information alone MUST NOT be used to gateway a message from a foreign (non-SMTP) mail system into an SMTP environment.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: The first host in the <reverse-path> was historically the host sending the MAIL command; today, source routes SHOULD NOT appear in the reverse-path.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: However, in general, the <forward-path> SHOULD contain only a mailbox and domain name, relying on the domain name system to supply routing information if required.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: The use of source routes is deprecated (see Appendix F.2); while servers MUST be prepared to receive and handle them as discussed in Section 3.3 and Appendix F.2, clients SHOULD NOT transmit them and this section is included in the current specification only to provide context.
actions: accept and process source route per Section 3.3 and Appendix F.2

statements.subject: message
statements.description: For relay purposes, the forward-path may be a source route of the form "@ONE,@TWO:JOE@THREE", where ONE, TWO, and THREE MUST be fully-qualified domain names.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: A server that is reached by means of a source route (e.g., its domain name appears first in the list in the forward-path) MUST remove its domain name from any forward-paths in which that domain name appears before forwarding the message and MAY remove all other source routing information.
actions: remove own domain name from every forward-path listing it before forwarding message

statements.subject: server
statements.description: The reverse-path SHOULD NOT be updated by servers conforming to this specification.
actions: do not modify reverse-path during message forwarding

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Conversely, SMTP servers MUST NOT derive final message routing information from message header fields.
actions: use only envelope forward-path for routing decisions, not message header fields

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If, contrary to the recommendations here, a relay host adds itself to the beginning of the list, it MUST use its name as known in the transport environment to which it is relaying the mail rather than that of the transport environment from which the mail came (if they are different).
actions: record own name as known in outbound transport environment when prepending to reverse-path

statements.subject: server
statements.description: This is another reason why servers needing to return a message SHOULD ignore the source route entirely and simply use the domain as specified in the Mailbox.
actions: use domain from Mailbox for return routing

statements.subject: endpoint
statements.description: In general, gateways between the Internet and other mail systems SHOULD attempt to preserve any layering semantics across the boundaries between the two mail systems involved.

statements.subject: smtp
statements.description: A few features of RFC 821 have proven to be problematic and SHOULD NOT be used in Internet mail.

statements.subject: session
statements.description: SMTP systems SHOULD NOT use it unless the server can authenticate the client.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: SMTP servers MUST continue to accept source route syntax as specified in the main body of this document and in RFC 1123.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: They MAY, if necessary, ignore the routes and utilize only the target domain in the address.

statements.subject: message
statements.description: If they do utilize the source route, the message MUST be sent to the first domain shown in the address.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: In particular, a server MUST NOT guess at shortcuts within the source route.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Clients SHOULD NOT utilize explicit source routing except under unusual circumstances, such as debugging or potentially relaying around firewall or mail system configuration errors.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: As discussed in Sections 3.1 and 4.1.1, EHLO SHOULD be used rather than HELO when the server will accept the former.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Servers MUST continue to accept and process HELO in order to support older clients.

statements.subject: participant
statements.description: It is deprecated and MUST NOT be used.

statements.subject: participant
statements.description: When dates are inserted into messages by SMTP clients or servers (e.g., in trace header fields), four-digit years MUST BE used.

statements.subject: client
statements.description: Clients SHOULD NOT provide SEND, SAML, or SOML as services.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: Servers MAY implement them.

statements.subject: server
statements.description: If they are implemented by servers, the implementation model specified in RFC 821 MUST be used and the command names MUST be published in the response to the EHLO command.
